A returnee under the proviso is deemed, for Article 6(b) purposes, to have migrated into India after 19 July 1948 — triggering the registration requirement
exceptions_and_qualifications: The bar in Article 7 overrides both Article 5 (the general test) and Article 6 (the migrant-into-India deeming rule) via its own non-obstante opening
The proviso's benefit is available only to those who returned under a lawful resettlement/permanent-return permit — informal or unauthorised return does not qualify
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Articles 6 and 7 as a linked pair governing Partition-era two-way migration — Article 6 deems certain in-migrants citizens, Article 7 deems certain out-migrants non-citizens, and the proviso to Article 7 is the narrow bridge back for people who left and then formally returned.

sections.title: Rights of citizenship of certain persons of Indian origin residing outside India
sections.raw_text: Notwithstanding anything in article 5, any person who or either of whose parents or any of whose grand-parents was born in India as defined in the Government of India Act, 1935 (as originally enacted), and who is ordinarily residing in any country outside India as so defined shall be deemed to be a citizen of India if he has been registered as a citizen of India by the diplomatic or consular representative of India in the country where he is for the time being residing on an application made by him therefor to such diplomatic or consular representative, whether before or after the commencement of this Constitution, in the form and manner prescribed by the Government of the Dominion of India or the Government of India.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 8 extends citizenship to the Indian diaspora of that era — people of Indian origin (by birth or ancestry, going back to a parent or grandparent) who were living abroad at the relevant time. Unlike Articles 5 and 6, which look at residence inside India, Article 8 lets such overseas persons become Indian citizens purely by registering with an Indian diplomatic or consular officer in the country where they were living, whether that registration happened before or after the Constitution commenced.
essential_elements: Ancestral-birth condition identical in structure to Article 6: self, parent, or grandparent born in undivided India
Ordinary residence in a country outside India (as defined by the 1935 Act) at the relevant time
Registration with an Indian diplomatic or consular representative abroad, in the prescribed form and manner, is the operative act that confers citizenship
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Article, again, operates notwithstanding Article 5 — it is a distinct, self-contained route to citizenship for the overseas Indian-origin population, not an application of the domicile test
Registration could validly occur either before or after the Constitution's commencement — the timing itself is not fatal, unlike the stricter cut-off dates in Articles 6 and 7
breakdown.how_to_read: Do not confuse Article 8's diaspora-registration route (a one-time historical mechanism operating around commencement) with the modern Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) scheme, which is a creature of the Citizenship Act, 1955 as amended, made under Article 11.

sections.title: Persons voluntarily acquiring citizenship of a foreign State not to be citizens
sections.raw_text: No person shall be a citizen of India by virtue of article 5, or be deemed to be a citizen of India by virtue of article 6 or article 8, if he has voluntarily acquired the citizenship of any foreign State.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 9 enforces India's single-citizenship principle at the constitutional threshold: anyone who had voluntarily taken up the citizenship of another country is disqualified from being treated as an Indian citizen under Articles 5, 6, or 8, no matter how strong their birth or ancestral connection to India otherwise was.
essential_elements: Applies specifically to disqualify citizenship claims that would otherwise arise under Articles 5, 6, or 8
The acquisition of foreign citizenship must be voluntary — an involuntary or automatic conferral by foreign law (without the person's choice) would not trigger this bar in the same way
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 9 does not itself regulate the loss of citizenship after a person has already become an Indian citizen and later acquires foreign citizenship — that is governed by the Citizenship Act, 1955 made under Article 11

Courts have had to interpret what counts as 'voluntary acquisition' in individual fact situations (e.g., automatic conferral of foreign nationality on marriage or by operation of foreign law without an affirmative act)
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Article 9 as a threshold bar operating only at the Article 5/6/8 citizenship-determination stage — for citizenship already vested and later placed in doubt by acquisition of a foreign passport, the operative law is the Citizenship Act, 1955, not this Article directly.

sections.title: Continuance of the rights of citizenship
sections.raw_text: Every person who is or is deemed to be a citizen of India under any of the foregoing provisions of this Part shall, subject to the provisions of any law that may be made by Parliament, continue to be such citizen.
key_terms: subject to law made by Parliament

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 10 provides continuity: once a person qualifies as a citizen under any of Articles 5 to 9, that citizenship persists going forward, unless and until Parliament makes a law that changes the position (for instance, providing for loss of citizenship in specified circumstances).
essential_elements: Citizenship, once established under Articles 5-9, is presumed to continue indefinitely
This continuance is expressly made subject to future Parliamentary law — it is not an unconditional guarantee immune from legislative modification
exceptions_and_qualifications: The qualifying phrase 'subject to the provisions of any law that may be made by Parliament' is what allows the Citizenship Act, 1955 to validly provide for termination of citizenship (e.g., on voluntary acquisition of another citizenship, or by an order of the Central Government) without being unconstitutional
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 10 is the constitutional bridge that lets ordinary citizenship law override the default continuance rule — always check the Citizenship Act, 1955 (and its amendments) for whether a particular person's citizenship has since been terminated, rather than assuming permanence purely from satisfying Articles 5-9.

sections.title: Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law
sections.raw_text: Nothing in the foregoing provisions of this Part shall derogate from the power of Parliament to make any provision with respect to the acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship.
key_terms: plenary power of Parliament over citizenship

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 11 is the Part's closing 'clear the decks' provision: it confirms that Articles 5 to 10 do not exhaust or limit Parliament's law-making power over citizenship. Parliament retains full authority to legislate on how citizenship is acquired (by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation) and how it is lost, and on any other citizenship-related matter — which is exactly the authority exercised through the Citizenship Act, 1955.
essential_elements: Parliament's power under Article 11 is plenary and not confined or cut down by the specific historical rules in Articles 5-10
Covers both acquisition and termination of citizenship, plus 'all other matters relating to citizenship'
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 11 is what makes the Citizenship Act, 1955 (and later amendments such as those dealing with Overseas Citizens of India, or citizenship by registration/naturalisation) constitutionally valid — without this Article, Parliament's power might have been seen as limited to filling gaps left by Articles 5-10 rather than freely legislating the whole subject
breakdown.how_to_read: Whenever a citizenship question falls outside the narrow historical scenarios of Articles 5-9 (e.g., birth after 1950, naturalisation, or loss of citizenship), the governing law is legislation made by Parliament under this Article — principally the Citizenship Act, 1955 — not the constitutional Articles themselves.

sections.title: Definition
sections.raw_text: In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires, "the State" includes the Government and Parliament of India and the Government and the Legislature of each of the States and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India.
key_terms: under the control of the Government of India

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 12 answers a foundational question for the entire Fundamental Rights Part: against whom can these rights be enforced? It defines 'the State' broadly — not just the Union and State Governments and Legislatures, but also 'local or other authorities' operating within India or under Indian Government control. This wide definition determines which bodies (e.g., municipalities, statutory corporations, universities, regulatory authorities) can be sued for violating a fundamental right.
essential_elements: 'The State' expressly includes the Government and Parliament of India
It also includes the Government and Legislature of each State
It extends to all local authorities (e.g., municipalities, panchayats) and 'other authorities' within India or under Central Government control
exceptions_and_qualifications: Courts have developed tests (e.g., deep and pervasive State control, functional/financial dependence on government) to decide whether a particular body — such as a statutory corporation or a government company — qualifies as 'other authorities' and is therefore bound by Part III

Purely private individuals and private bodies not meeting these tests generally fall outside Article 12 and cannot be directly sued for fundamental rights violations (though some rights, like Article 17 and Article 23, expressly bind private persons too)
breakdown.how_to_read: Always check Article 12 first before invoking any fundamental right against a body other than the Union or a State Government directly — if the body is not 'the State' within this definition (as judicially elaborated), the fundamental-rights remedy under Article 32/226 may not be available against it at all.

sections.title: Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the fundamental rights
sections.raw_text: (1) All laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void. (2) The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void. (3) In this article, unless the context otherwise requires,— (a) "law" includes any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law; (b) "laws in force" includes laws passed or made by a Legislature or other competent authority in the territory of India before the commencement of this Constitution and not previously repealed, notwithstanding that any such law or any part thereof may not be then in operation either at all or in particular areas. (4) Nothing in this article shall apply to any amendment of this Constitution made under article 368.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 13 is the enforcement teeth of Part III: it makes both old (pre-1950) laws and any future law void to the extent they conflict with fundamental rights. Clause (1) strikes down pre-constitutional laws that clash with Part III (only to the extent of the conflict — the rest survives, per the doctrine of severability). Clause (2) is a forward-looking bar preventing the State from ever validly making a law that takes away or abridges a fundamental right; any such law is void to that extent. Clause (3) gives 'law' and 'laws in force' very wide definitions, sweeping in not just statutes but ordinances, rules, regulations, notifications, and even custom or usage having legal force. Clause (4), added later, clarifies that constitutional amendments made under Article 368 are not 'law' for Article 13 purposes — insulating amendments from being struck down merely for being inconsistent with a fundamental right (though the basic structure doctrine still constrains amendments through other means).
essential_elements: Clause (1): pre-constitutional inconsistent laws are void to the extent of inconsistency (not wholly void)
Clause (2): the State is barred from making any law that takes away or abridges Part III rights; violating laws are void to the extent of the contravention
Clause (3)(a)-(b): 'law' and 'laws in force' are defined expansively to include subordinate legislation and custom/usage with legal force
Clause (4): constitutional amendments under Article 368 are excluded from Article 13's reach
exceptions_and_qualifications: The doctrine of eclipse allows a pre-constitutional law inconsistent with a fundamental right to remain 'eclipsed' (dormant, unenforceable against citizens) rather than being wiped out entirely — it can revive if the relevant right is later amended away, though this doctrine is generally understood to apply differently to post-constitutional laws

Clause (4)'s exclusion of constitutional amendments does not mean amendments are wholly beyond judicial review — the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati) independently limits Parliament's amending power under Article 368 itself
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 13 is the provision to cite whenever arguing that a statute, rule, notification, or even a custom is constitutionally void for violating a Part III right — but remember clause (4) means you cannot use Article 13 alone to challenge a constitutional amendment; for that, the basic structure doctrine under Article 368 jurisprudence is the relevant framework.

sections.title: Equality before law
sections.raw_text: The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 14 guarantees two related but distinct ideas to every person (not just citizens) within India: 'equality before the law' (a negative concept, borrowed from British constitutional tradition, meaning no one is above the law and all are equally subject to the ordinary law of the land) and 'equal protection of the laws' (a more positive, American-influenced concept, meaning like persons should be treated alike under the law). Together they form the bedrock non-discrimination guarantee of the Constitution, enforceable against 'the State' as defined in Article 12.
essential_elements: Applies to 'any person' — not limited to citizens, unlike some other Part III rights
'Equality before law' = no person is above the law; the law applies equally to all, including the State's own officials
'Equal protection of the laws' = persons in similar circumstances should be treated similarly, and the law itself must not be arbitrarily discriminatory
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 14 does not forbid all classification by law — it only forbids 'class legislation' that is arbitrary; reasonable classification is permitted if it satisfies a twin test: (i) the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia distinguishing grouped persons from others, and (ii) that differentia must have a rational nexus to the object sought to be achieved by the law

Article 14 has also been read (post-Maneka Gandhi and E.P. Royappa) to strike at arbitrariness itself — an arbitrary State action can violate Article 14 even without a classic 'classification' problem
breakdown.how_to_read: When pleading Article 14, always frame the argument through the two-limb reasonable-classification test (intelligible differentia + rational nexus) if challenging a classification, or through the broader 'arbitrariness' strand if challenging discretionary/arbitrary State action that doesn't fit the classification mould.

sections.title: Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
sections.raw_text: (1) The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them. (2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to— (a) access to shops, public restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment; or (b) the use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds or dedicated to the use of the general public. (3) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any special provision for women and children. (4) Nothing in this article or in clause (2) of article 29 shall prevent the State from making any special provision for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes. (5) Nothing in this article or in sub-clause (g) of clause (1) of article 19 shall prevent the State from making any special provision, by law, for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes or the Scheduled Tribes in so far as such special provisions relate to their admission to educational institutions including private educational institutions, whether aided or unaided by the State, other than the minority educational institutions referred to in clause (1) of article 30. (6) Nothing in this article or sub-clause (g) of clause (1) of article 19 or clause (2) of article 29 shall prevent the State from making,— (a) any special provision for the advancement of any economically weaker sections of citizens other than the classes mentioned in clauses (4) and (5); and (b) any special provision for the advancement of any economically weaker sections of citizens other than the classes mentioned in clauses (4) and (5) in so far as such special provisions relate to their admission to educational institutions including private educational institutions, whether aided or unaided by the State, other than the minority educational institutions referred to in clause (1) of article 30, which in the case of reservation would be in addition to the existing reservations and subject to a maximum of ten per cent. of the total seats in each category. Explanation.—For the purposes of this article and article 16, "economically weaker sections" shall be such as may be notified by the State from time to time on the basis of family income and other indicators of economic disadvantage.
key_terms: grounds only of religion race caste sex place of birth
special provision for women and children

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 15 is Article 14's specific application against the historically most dangerous grounds of discrimination. Clauses (1)-(2) forbid the State (clause 1) and even private persons controlling public-facing establishments/resorts (clause 2) from discriminating against a citizen purely on religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. But the Article is equally famous for its enabling clauses: (3) permits affirmative special provisions for women and children; (4) and (5) permit reservations/special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes and for SCs/STs, including in educational institutions; and (6), added in 2019, extends similar (capped at 10%) affirmative provisions to economically weaker sections (EWS) not otherwise covered by (4)/(5), based on notified economic-disadvantage criteria.
essential_elements: Discrimination must be 'on grounds only of' the listed characteristics — if a classification uses an additional, non-listed factor together with a listed one, Article 15(1)/(2) is not automatically violated
Clause (2)'s prohibition on discriminatory access extends beyond the State to any establishment maintained wholly/partly from State funds or dedicated to public use
Clauses (3)-(6) are not exceptions carved out of a violation but express constitutional permissions ('nothing in this article shall prevent') for affirmative action
exceptions_and_qualifications: The EWS reservation under clause (6) is capped at a maximum of ten per cent and must be 'in addition to' existing reservations, and expressly excludes classes already covered by clauses (4) and (5)
Minority educational institutions referred to in Article 30(1) are excluded from the special educational-admission provisions in clauses (5) and (6)
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish the prohibitory clauses (1)-(2), which are the sword against discrimination, from the enabling clauses (3)-(6), which are shields protecting affirmative-action legislation from being struck down as reverse discrimination — a law under clause (4), (5), or (6) does not need to separately satisfy the Article 14 reasonable-classification test in the same way ordinary legislation does, because the Constitution itself has pre-authorised this category of classification.

sections.title: Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment
sections.raw_text: (1) There shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. (2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office under the State. (3) Nothing in this article shall prevent Parliament from making any law prescribing, in regard to a class or classes of employment or appointment to an office under the Government of, or any local or other authority within, a State or Union territory, any requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory prior to such employment or appointment. (4) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for the reservation of appointments or posts in favour of any backward class of citizens which, in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services under the State. (4A) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for reservation in matters of promotion, with consequential seniority, to any class or classes of posts in the services under the State in favour of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes which, in the opinion of the State, are not adequately represented in the services under the State. (4B) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from considering any unfilled vacancies of a year which are reserved for being filled up in that year in accordance with any provision for reservation made under clause (4) or clause (4A) as a separate class of vacancies to be filled up in any succeeding year or years and such class of vacancies shall not be considered together with the vacancies of the year in which they are being filled up for determining the ceiling of fifty per cent. reservation on total number of vacancies of that year. (5) Nothing in this article shall affect the operation of any law which provides that the incumbent of an office in connection with the affairs of any religious or denominational institution or any member of the governing body thereof shall be a person professing a particular religion or belonging to a particular denomination. (6) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for the reservation of appointments or posts in favour of any economically weaker sections of citizens other than the classes mentioned in clause (4), in addition to the existing reservation and subject to a maximum of ten per cent. of the posts in each category.
key_terms: equality of opportunity in public employment

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 16 applies the Article 14/15 equality principle specifically to jobs 'under the State' — government and public sector employment. Clause (1) guarantees equal opportunity; clause (2) forbids discrimination on the listed grounds (which here additionally include 'descent' and 'residence' beyond Article 15's list). The remaining clauses are the constitutional machinery for reservation policy in public employment: clause (3) lets Parliament impose State/UT residence requirements for certain posts; clause (4) permits reservation for backward classes inadequately represented in State services; (4A) extends this to promotions (with consequential seniority) for SCs/STs; (4B) allows unfilled reserved vacancies to be carried forward to future years without counting against the 50% ceiling for that later year; clause (5) preserves religious-denomination-based eligibility rules for offices tied to running religious institutions; and clause (6), added alongside Article 15(6), permits a further 10% EWS reservation.
essential_elements: Clause (1)-(2) establish the baseline: equal opportunity and non-discrimination on listed grounds in public employment
Clause (3) is the sole ground on which residence-based restriction is permitted, and only by Parliament's law, not State legislatures

Clauses (4), (4A), (4B), and (6) are successive enabling provisions permitting different forms of reservation, each with its own conditions (inadequate representation, promotion-specific consequential seniority, carry-forward treatment, and the EWS cap respectively)
exceptions_and_qualifications: The judicially evolved 50% ceiling on total reservations (from Indra Sawhant/Mandal jurisprudence) is not textually stated in Article 16 itself (except implicitly via clause 4B's cross-reference) but has been treated as a general limit, subject to the EWS clause (6) reservation being treated somewhat differently in recent jurisprudence
Clause (5)'s exception for denominational institution offices is narrow — confined to offices connected with the affairs of the religious/denominational institution itself
breakdown.how_to_read: When analysing a public employment reservation scheme, identify precisely which enabling clause it rests on — backward-class entry reservation (4), SC/ST promotion reservation (4A), carry-forward vacancy treatment (4B), or EWS reservation (6) — since each has distinct conditions and the 50% ceiling discourse applies differently to each.

sections.title: Abolition of Untouchability
sections.raw_text: "Untouchability" is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of "Untouchability" shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.
key_terms: enforcement of disability arising out of Untouchability

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 17 is one of the few fundamental rights that operates directly against private individuals, not just the State. It abolishes the practice of 'Untouchability' in any form, and criminalises the enforcement of any disability that arises from it — meaning ordinary legislation (principally the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955, and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989) gives this constitutional abolition concrete penal teeth.
essential_elements: The abolition and prohibition operate horizontally — enforceable against private persons, not merely 'the State'

The Article itself does not define 'Untouchability' in detail (deliberately using the term in its historically understood, socially oppressive sense) or prescribe the specific punishment; both are left to ordinary law
exceptions_and_qualifications: Article 17's self-executing abolition is reinforced, not exhausted, by statutory law — the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (originally the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955) and later special legislation provide the actual offences and penalties contemplated by the phrase 'in accordance with law'
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 17 is a rare example of a fundamental right directly binding private citizens — when a discrimination claim arises from caste-based social exclusion practised by private individuals (not the State), this is the Article to invoke, read together with the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.

sections.title: Abolition of titles
sections.raw_text: (1) No title, not being a military or academic distinction, shall be conferred by the State. (2) No citizen of India shall accept any title from any foreign State. (3) No person who is not a citizen of India shall, while he holds any office of profit or trust under the State, accept without the consent of the President any title from any foreign State. (4) No person holding any office of profit or trust under the State shall, without the consent of the President, accept any present, emolument, or office of any kind from or under any foreign State.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 18 reflects the framers' rejection of hereditary/feudal titles (like the colonial-era 'Rai Bahadur' or 'Sir') as instruments of State-conferred hierarchy. Clause (1) bars the Indian State itself from conferring such titles, while carving out ordinary military and academic distinctions (e.g., gallantry awards, degrees). Clauses (2)-(4) then guard against foreign entanglement and undue influence: citizens cannot accept titles from foreign States at all; non-citizens holding a State office of profit/trust need presidential consent to accept a foreign title; and anyone holding such a State office needs presidential consent even to accept a foreign present, payment, or office.
essential_elements: Clause (1): the State cannot confer non-military, non-academic titles — this is what underlies the National Awards (Bharat Ratna, Padma awards) being formally styled as non-titular civilian 'awards' or 'distinctions', not titles, following constitutional and judicial clarification (Balaji Raghavan case)
Clauses (2)-(4) form an escalating scheme regulating foreign honours/benefits based on citizenship and whether the recipient holds a State office of profit or trust
exceptions_and_qualifications: Military and academic distinctions are expressly excluded from clause (1)'s bar and may be freely conferred by the State
Presidential consent under clauses (3) and (4) is a case-specific safeguard, not a blanket permission — each acceptance requires its own consent
breakdown.how_to_read: Cite Article 18 whenever a dispute involves the constitutionality of State-conferred honours (distinguishing genuine 'titles' from permitted awards/distinctions) or a foreign-honours-acceptance controversy involving a public office-holder — the operative question is always whether presidential consent under clauses (3)/(4) was sought where required.

sections.title: Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc.
sections.raw_text: (1) All citizens shall have the right— (a) to freedom of speech and expression; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) to form associations or unions or co-operative societies; (d) to move freely throughout the territory of India; (e) to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India; and (g) to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business. (2) Nothing in sub-clause (a) of clause (1) shall affect the operation of any existing law, or prevent the State from making any law, in so far as such law imposes reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence. (3) Nothing in sub-clause (b) of the said clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order, reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause. (4) Nothing in sub-clause (c) of the said clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order or morality, reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause. (5) Nothing in sub-clauses (d) and (e) of the said clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, reasonable restrictions on the exercise of any of the rights conferred by the said sub-clauses either in the interests of the general public or for the protection of the interests of any Scheduled Tribe. (6) Nothing in sub-clause (g) of the said clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, in the interests of the general public, reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause, and, in particular, nothing in the said sub-clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it relates to, or prevent the State from making any law relating to,— (i) the professional or technical qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade or business, or (ii) the carrying on by the State, or by a corporation owned or controlled by the State, of any trade, business, industry or service, whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.
key_terms: State monopoly in trade or business

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 19(1) is the Constitution's core bundle of individual liberties for citizens: speech and expression, peaceable unarmed assembly, forming associations/unions/co-operative societies, free movement throughout India, residing and settling anywhere in India, and practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade, or business (the original property-right sub-clause (f) was removed in 1978, when the right to property was demoted from a fundamental right to Article 300A). None of these six freedoms is absolute — clauses (2) through (6) are mirror-image 'restriction clauses', one for each surviving sub-clause, letting the State impose 'reasonable restrictions' on specified public-interest grounds. Crucially, the grounds differ freedom by freedom (speech's grounds under clause 2 are the most numerous and specific, including sovereignty/integrity, State security, foreign relations, public order, decency/morality, contempt of court, defamation, and incitement to an offence), so each sub-clause must be checked against its own tailored restriction clause.
essential_elements: Clause (1) lists six substantive freedoms: speech/expression (a), peaceable assembly (b), association/union/co-operative society (c), movement (d), residence (e), and profession/occupation/trade/business (g)
Each restriction clause (2)-(6) is specific to one sub-clause and lists its own distinct permissible grounds for restriction
Restrictions must be 'reasonable' — an independent, judicially reviewable standard, not merely any restriction the State chooses to impose
Clause (6) additionally permits State monopolies (wholly or partly excluding citizens) in trade, business, industry, or service
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-clause (f) (the original right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property) was omitted by the Forty-fourth Amendment Act, 1978, and is no longer a Part III fundamental right — property is now protected only as a constitutional (not fundamental) right under Article 300A

The 'reasonableness' of a restriction is tested by courts considering the nature of the right, the extent and urgency of the evil sought to be remedied, proportionality of the restriction, and the manner of its imposition — not left to unreviewable legislative discretion
These six freedoms are available only to citizens, unlike Articles 14, 20, 21, and 22 which extend more broadly to 'persons'
breakdown.how_to_read: When analysing an Article 19 challenge, always identify (i) which specific sub-clause of clause (1) is invoked, (ii) whether the challenged restriction falls within that sub-clause's own tailored restriction clause (2)-(6), and (iii) whether the restriction is 'reasonable' on the facts — a restriction valid for one sub-clause's grounds cannot be borrowed to justify restricting a different freedom.

sections.title: Protection in respect of conviction for offences
sections.raw_text: (1) No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the Act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. (2) No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. (3) No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.
key_terms: protection against ex post facto law

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 20 provides three distinct criminal-law protections available to 'any person' (citizen or not), all non-suspendable even during a proclamation of Emergency. Clause (1) bars ex post facto criminal laws — a person cannot be convicted for an act that was not an offence when committed, nor punished more severely than the law in force at that time allowed. Clause (2) is the double jeopardy protection — no repeated prosecution and punishment for the same offence once already prosecuted and punished for it. Clause (3) is the privilege against self-incrimination — an accused person cannot be compelled to testify against themselves.
essential_elements: Clause (1): applies only to the imposition of criminal liability/penalty for an act not an offence at the time, or a penalty exceeding what the law then prescribed — it does not bar retrospective civil laws or procedural changes
Clause (2): 'prosecuted and punished' requires both a prior prosecution AND punishment for the very same offence — a mere prior prosecution that did not result in punishment does not trigger this bar

Clause (3): the compulsion must be to be a witness 'against himself' — it protects against compelled self-incriminatory testimonial communication, not all forms of evidence gathering (e.g., producing certain physical evidence, subject to scrutiny)
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (1) does not prevent a change in criminal procedure being applied retrospectively — only substantive offence-creation and penalty-enhancement are barred retrospectively

Clause (2)'s double jeopardy protection is narrower than some other jurisdictions' — it requires actual prior punishment, not merely a prior trial or acquittal (contrast with the statutory protection in the Cr.P.C./BNSS against second trial after acquittal or conviction)
Article 20's three protections are among the very few fundamental rights that Article 359 does not permit to be suspended during a National Emergency
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 20 is the standard citation for challenging retrospective criminal legislation (clause 1), a second prosecution for an identical offence already punished (clause 2), or coerced confessions/testimony (clause 3) — always confirm these protections remain available even during an Emergency, unlike most other Part III rights.

sections.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
sections.raw_text: No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 21, in just one sentence, has become the single most expansively interpreted provision of the Indian Constitution. On its face, it only guarantees that the State cannot deprive any person of life or personal liberty except through a 'procedure established by law' — originally read (in A.K. Gopalan) as merely requiring that some valid enacted procedure exist, however harsh. This changed fundamentally after Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), which held that the 'procedure' itself must be fair, just, and reasonable (effectively importing a due-process-like standard) and that Articles 14, 19, and 21 are interlinked, not mutually exclusive silos. Since then, courts have read into 'life' and 'personal liberty' a vast range of unenumerated rights — including privacy, dignity, livelihood, health, a clean environment, speedy trial, legal aid, and shelter, among many others.
essential_elements: Applies to 'any person' (not just citizens), and protects both 'life' and 'personal liberty'
Deprivation must follow a 'procedure established by law' — post-Maneka Gandhi, that procedure must itself be fair, just, and reasonable, not merely enacted
The right has been judicially expanded to encompass numerous unenumerated rights considered essential to a life of dignity
exceptions_and_qualifications: Pre-Maneka Gandhi jurisprudence (A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras) treated 'procedure established by law' as a narrower guarantee than American 'due process of law', focused on mere existence of enacted procedure rather than its substantive fairness — this narrow view no longer represents the law
The right to privacy was expressly recognised as intrinsic to Article 21 (and Part III generally) in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), a landmark 9-judge bench decision
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Article 21 as the Constitution's residuary reservoir of substantive liberty — when no other specific fundamental right precisely fits a claim involving bodily autonomy, dignity, livelihood, or procedural fairness in deprivation of liberty, Article 21 (read with the post-Maneka Gandhi fairness standard) is very likely the applicable provision, and always check whether the 'procedure' under challenge would itself survive a fairness/reasonableness test, not merely whether a procedure exists on paper.

sections.title: Right to education
sections.raw_text: The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 21A, inserted in 2002, elevates elementary education from a mere Directive Principle (it was previously only aspirational under Article 45) to an enforceable fundamental right. It obliges the State to provide free and compulsory education to every child aged six to fourteen, with the precise implementation manner left to be determined by law — which Parliament did through the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (the RTE Act).
essential_elements: The right is age-bound: specifically children between six and fourteen years
The obligation is on 'the State' to provide education that is both free and compulsory
The 'manner' of providing this education is left to be determined by law — i.e., this Article is not fully self-executing without implementing legislation
exceptions_and_qualifications: Education for children below six or above fourteen (e.g., early childhood care, or secondary/higher education) is not directly guaranteed as a fundamental right under this Article, though early childhood care up to age six is separately addressed as a Directive Principle under the amended Article 45

The RTE Act, 2009 is the primary implementing legislation giving Article 21A operational content — including provisions on neighbourhood schools, 25% reservation for disadvantaged groups in private unaided schools, and prohibition of detention/expulsion up to a certain class
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 21A must always be read together with the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 for its practical content — the Article establishes the fundamental right in principle, but the Act supplies the operative rules (admission age, curriculum standards, private-school obligations, etc.).

sections.title: Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases
sections.raw_text: (1) No person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest nor shall he be denied the right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of his choice. (2) Every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the magistrate and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate. (3) Nothing in clauses (1) and (2) shall apply— (a) to any person who for the time being is an enemy alien; or (b) to any person who is arrested or detained under any law providing for preventive detention. (4) No law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless— (a) an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as, Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention: Provided that nothing in this sub-clause shall authorise the detention of any person beyond the maximum period prescribed by any law made by Parliament under sub-clause (b) of clause (7); or (b) such person is detained in accordance with the provisions of any law made by Parliament under sub-clauses (a) and (b) of clause (7). (5) When any person is detained in pursuance of an order made under any law providing for preventive detention, the authority making the order shall, as soon as may be, communicate to such person the grounds on which the order has been made and shall afford him the earliest opportunity of making a representation against the order. (6) Nothing in clause (5) shall require the authority making any such order as is referred to in that clause to disclose facts which such authority considers to be against the public interest to disclose. (7) Parliament may by law prescribe— (a) the circumstances under which, and the class or classes of cases in which, a person may be detained for a period longer than three months under any law providing for preventive detention without obtaining the opinion of an Advisory Board in accordance with the provisions of sub-clause (a) of clause (4); (b) the maximum period for which any person may in any class or classes of cases be detained under any law providing for preventive detention; and (c) the procedure to be followed by an Advisory Board in an inquiry under sub-clause (a) of clause (4).

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 22 splits arrest/detention protections into two very different tracks. Clauses (1)-(2) protect ordinary (punitive) arrestees: the right to be told the grounds of arrest promptly, the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice, and the right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours (excluding travel time), with no custody beyond that period without magisterial authorisation. Clause (3) carves out two categories from these protections entirely — enemy aliens, and anyone arrested/detained under a preventive detention law. Clauses (4)-(7) then set up a separate, more limited protective scheme specifically for preventive detention (confinement to prevent anticipated future harm, not to punish a past offence): ordinarily capping detention beyond three months unless an Advisory Board of High-Court-qualified persons certifies sufficient cause, requiring communication of detention grounds and an opportunity to make a representation (subject to a public-interest non-disclosure carve-out), and leaving Parliament to legislate the finer procedural details.
essential_elements: Clauses (1)-(2) are the baseline protections for ordinary arrest: grounds disclosure, right to counsel, and 24-hour magistrate production
Clause (3) removes these baseline protections entirely for enemy aliens and for persons held under preventive detention laws

Clauses (4)-(7) substitute a different, narrower set of safeguards specifically for preventive detention: the three-month Advisory Board check, grounds communication, representation opportunity (clause 5), and a public-interest non-disclosure exception (clause 6)
exceptions_and_qualifications: Preventive detention is a striking constitutional anomaly — confinement without trial, justified by anticipated rather than committed wrongdoing — and Article 22's own safeguards for it are considerably weaker than the ordinary-arrest protections in clauses (1)-(2)

A Forty-fourth Amendment Act, 1978 substitution of clause (4) (shortening the default period to two months and reworking the Advisory Board composition) was enacted but has never been brought into force by notification, so the original three-month scheme printed here remains the operative law
The public-interest non-disclosure carve-out in clause (6) has been strictly construed by courts to prevent it from swallowing the representation right in clause (5)
breakdown.how_to_read: Always separate an Article 22 analysis into the two tracks — first ask whether the detention is ordinary/punitive (clauses 1-2 apply in full) or preventive (clauses 3-7 apply instead, with the specific procedural safeguards of clauses 4-7 substituting for clauses 1-2) — and note that the harsher, unnotified 1978 amendment to clause (4) is not yet in force, so the original three-month/Advisory-Board text governs in practice.

sections.title: Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
sections.raw_text: (1) Traffic in human beings and begar and other similar forms of forced labour are prohibited and any contravention of this provision shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law. (2) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from imposing compulsory service for public purposes, and in imposing such service the State shall not make any discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class or any of them.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 23, like Article 17, operates horizontally — directly against private individuals, not merely the State. It prohibits human trafficking and 'begar' (a traditional term for labour exacted without payment) and other forms of forced labour, making any contravention a punishable offence. Clause (2) carves out compulsory public service (such as conscription-type civic duties) as permissible, but even here the State cannot discriminate in imposing that service on grounds only of religion, race, caste, or class.
essential_elements: Prohibition covers human trafficking and begar/forced labour in any similar form, enforceable against private persons as well as the State
Contravention is made a punishable offence, with the specific offence and penalty left to ordinary law
Clause (2) permits State-imposed compulsory service for public purposes, subject to a non-discrimination proviso on the listed grounds
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Supreme Court in People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (1982) held that paying wages below the statutory minimum wage amounts to 'forced labour' under Article 23, significantly widening the provision's reach beyond literal bonded labour
The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 is the principal legislation giving Article 23 further statutory content
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 23 is a rare horizontally-enforceable right — use it directly against private employers or individuals engaged in trafficking, bonded labour, or forced/underpaid labour, and remember the expanded 'forced labour' definition covering sub-minimum-wage work established in the PUDR case.

sections.title: Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc.
sections.raw_text: No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 24 bars the employment of children below fourteen years in factories, mines, or any other hazardous work, protecting children from exploitative and dangerous labour during their formative years. Like Articles 17 and 23, it is understood to operate against both State and private employers.
essential_elements: The prohibition applies specifically to children below fourteen years of age
It covers employment in factories, mines, and 'any other hazardous employment' — a category courts and legislation have further defined
It operates against private employers as well as the State
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (renamed and amended as the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act) is the principal statute implementing this Article, specifying the list of hazardous occupations and processes and providing enforcement mechanisms

Non-hazardous family-enterprise or artistic work by children, subject to statutory conditions, has historically been treated differently under the implementing legislation, though this remains a contested policy area
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 24 together with Article 21A (right to education) and Article 39(e)-(f) (Directive Principles on child welfare) as a cluster of child-protection provisions, and consult the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act for the operative list of hazardous occupations/processes.

sections.title: Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion
sections.raw_text: (1) Subject to public order, morality and health and to the other provisions of this Part, all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practice and propagate religion. (2) Nothing in this article shall affect the operation of any existing law or prevent the State from making any law— (a) regulating or restricting any economic, financial, political or other secular activity which may be associated with religious practice; (b) providing for social welfare and reform or the throwing open of Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus. Explanation I.—The wearing and carrying of kirpans shall be deemed to be included in the profession of the Sikh religion. Explanation II.—In sub-clause (b) of clause (2), the reference to Hindus shall be construed as including a reference to persons professing the Sikh, Jaina or Buddhist religion, and the reference to Hindu religious institutions shall be construed accordingly.
key_terms: secular activity associated with religious practice
throwing open of Hindu religious institutions

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 25 guarantees every person — not just citizens — freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practice, and propagate their religion, though this is expressly made 'subject to public order, morality and health' and to the other Part III rights. Clause (2) preserves the State's power to regulate secular activities merely associated with religious practice (e.g., economic or political aspects of a religious institution's operation) and to enact social-welfare/reform laws, including opening Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus. Explanation I specifically protects a Sikh's wearing and carrying of a kirpan as part of religious profession. Explanation II clarifies that wherever clause (2)(b) refers to 'Hindus' and 'Hindu religious institutions', this is deemed to include Sikhs, Jains, and Buddhists and their institutions — reflecting the historical (and still debated) constitutional classification of these communities for this specific purpose.
essential_elements: The right belongs to 'all persons' and covers three distinct freedoms: freedom of conscience, and the rights to profess, practice, and propagate religion
The right is expressly subject to public order, morality, health, and the rest of Part III — it is not absolute
Clause (2)(a) preserves State power over secular activities merely associated with religion (e.g., managing temple finances)
Clause (2)(b) preserves State power for social welfare/reform and opening Hindu (and by Explanation II, Sikh/Jain/Buddhist) religious institutions to all classes
exceptions_and_qualifications: 'Propagate' has been judicially construed to mean transmitting or spreading one's own religious beliefs through exposition, not a right to forcibly convert another person (Rev. Stanislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh)

Explanation II's inclusion of Sikhs, Jains, and Buddhists within 'Hindus' is limited strictly to clause (2)(b)'s social-welfare/temple-access purpose — it does not mean these communities are treated as Hindus for all other constitutional or legal purposes
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 25 is the starting point for any freedom-of-religion analysis — always separate the core religious/conscience claim (protected, subject to public order/morality/health) from any 'secular activity merely associated with' the religious practice (which the State can regulate under clause 2(a)) — this distinction (the 'essential religious practices' test) is the recurring battleground in Indian religious-freedom litigation.

sections.title: Freedom to manage religious affairs
sections.raw_text: Subject to public order, morality and health, every religious denomination or any section thereof shall have the right— (a) to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes; (b) to manage its own affairs in matters of religion; (c) to own and acquire movable and immovable property; and (d) to administer such property in accordance with law.
key_terms: right to own and acquire property (religious institutions)

breakdown.plain_summary: While Article 25 protects the individual's freedom of religion, Article 26 protects the collective/institutional freedom of a 'religious denomination' (or a section of one) — again subject to public order, morality, and health. It guarantees four specific rights: establishing and maintaining religious and charitable institutions, managing the denomination's own religious affairs, owning and acquiring property, and administering that property, though the last right is qualified by 'in accordance with law' (meaning ordinary property/administration law can regulate how such property is managed, even though the right to manage religious affairs proper is more strongly insulated).
essential_elements: The right-holder is a 'religious denomination or any section thereof', not merely an individual — courts have developed a specific test for what qualifies as a 'religious denomination' (a common faith, common organisation, and a distinctive name)
Sub-clause (b) — managing 'matters of religion' — is the most strongly protected limb, closely tied to the 'essential religious practices' doctrine

Sub-clause (d) — administering property — is explicitly made subject to ordinary law, unlike sub-clause (b), giving the State greater regulatory latitude over property administration than over core religious affairs
exceptions_and_qualifications: The distinction between 'matters of religion' (protected, largely insulated from ordinary regulation) and 'secular'/administrative matters merely associated with religion (regulable by the State, especially given sub-clause (d)'s 'in accordance with law' qualifier) is the central interpretive battleground under this Article, mirroring the same essential-practices analysis under Article 25
breakdown.how_to_read: When a religious institution's internal governance is challenged, ask first whether the matter is a genuinely 'essential religious practice'/'matter of religion' under sub-clause (b) (strongly protected) or a property-administration matter under sub-clause (d) (subject to ordinary regulatory law) — the answer to this threshold question usually decides the case.

sections.title: Freedom as to payment of taxes for promotion of any particular religion
sections.raw_text: No person shall be compelled to pay any taxes, the proceeds of which are specifically appropriated in payment of expenses for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion or religious denomination.
key_terms: tax for promotion of a particular religion

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 27 embodies religious neutrality in public finance: no one can be compelled to pay a tax whose proceeds are specifically earmarked to promote or maintain a particular religion or denomination. This targets 'tax' (a compulsory levy for general public purposes) specifically — a general grant-in-aid or a 'fee' charged for specific services rendered to a religious institution (e.g., regulatory or administrative fees) is treated differently and does not automatically fall foul of this Article.
essential_elements: The bar applies to 'taxes' whose proceeds are specifically appropriated for promoting or maintaining a particular religion or denomination

General taxation that merely happens to fund composite State expenditure (which might incidentally benefit religious institutions among many other things) does not violate this Article, since there is no specific appropriation for a particular religion
exceptions_and_qualifications: Courts distinguish a 'tax' (compulsory exaction for general public purposes, no direct quid pro quo) from a 'fee' (a charge for specific services rendered, e.g., regulating or supervising a temple's secular administration), and fees of the latter kind have generally been upheld as not attracting Article 27's bar
breakdown.how_to_read: Article 27 is narrowly targeted — before invoking it, confirm the levy in question is genuinely a 'tax' with proceeds specifically earmarked for a particular religion's promotion/maintenance, rather than a general tax or a regulatory fee for secular administrative services connected to a religious institution.

sections.title: Freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in certain educational institutions
sections.raw_text: (1) No religious instruction shall be provided in any educational institution wholly maintained out of State funds. (2) Nothing in clause (1) shall apply to an educational institution which is administered by the State but has been established under any endowment or trust which requires that religious instruction shall be imparted in such institution. (3) No person attending any educational institution recognised by the State or receiving aid out of State funds shall be required to take part in any religious instruction that may be imparted in such institution or to attend any religious worship that may be conducted in such institution or in any premises attached thereto unless such person or, if such person is a minor, his guardian has given his consent thereto.
key_terms: consent for religious instruction or worship

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 28 addresses religion in education across a spectrum of institution types. Clause (1) flatly bars religious instruction in any institution wholly maintained out of State funds — full State funding means full religious neutrality. Clause (2) carves out an exception: if the State administers an institution that was established under a trust/endowment specifically requiring religious instruction (e.g., a formerly private religious college later taken over by the State but bound by its founding trust terms), that requirement can continue. Clause (3) covers a third category — institutions merely 'recognised' by the State or receiving State aid (but not wholly State-maintained) — where religious instruction/worship may occur, but no student (or, if a minor, their guardian) can be compelled to participate without consent.
essential_elements: Clause (1): wholly State-maintained institutions — religious instruction is completely barred
Clause (2): State-administered institutions bound by a founding trust/endowment requiring religious instruction — the exception preserves that requirement

Clause (3): State-recognised or State-aided (but not wholly State-run) institutions — religious instruction/worship may occur, but attendance/participation requires the student's (or minor's guardian's) consent
exceptions_and_qualifications: The three clauses create a graduated scheme based on the degree of State involvement (wholly funded vs. State-administered-but-trust-bound vs. merely recognised/aided) — the applicable rule depends entirely on correctly categorising the institution
Consent under clause (3) must be free and can be withheld even after initial enrolment, protecting ongoing rather than merely one-time choice
breakdown.how_to_read: When analysing a religious-instruction dispute in an educational institution, first classify the institution correctly among the three categories (wholly State-funded / State-administered-but-endowment-bound / merely recognised-or-aided) — the entire Article 28 analysis turns on this classification, and clause (3)'s consent requirement is the most commonly litigated limb in practice.

sections.title: Protection of interests of minorities
sections.raw_text:
29. Protection of interests of minorities.—(1) Any section of the citizens residing in the territory of India or any part thereof having a distinct language, script or culture of its own shall have the right to conserve the same.
(2) No citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them.
key_terms: right to conserve distinct language script or culture
denial of admission to educational institutions

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 29 protects the cultural identity of any group of citizens — not just religious or linguistic 'minorities' in the numerical sense, but any section with a distinct language, script, or culture. Clause (1) gives them a right to conserve that identity. Clause (2) is a separate, individual-facing guarantee: no citizen (of any community, majority or minority) can be refused admission to a State-run or State-aided educational institution purely on grounds of religion, race, caste, or language.
essential_elements: Clause (1): applies to any 'section of citizens', not exclusively religious or linguistic minorities — the group must have a distinct language, script, or culture of its own.
Clause (1): confers a right to conserve that language, script, or culture — protecting cultural continuity against forced assimilation.
Clause (2): protects the individual citizen, of any community, from denial of admission to a State-maintained or State-aided educational institution.
Clause (2)'s bar operates only where the denial rests on grounds only of religion, race, caste, or language (or a combination of only those grounds).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (2) does not bar reasonable, non-discriminatory admission criteria (merit, reserved seats under Article 15(4)/(5)) — only denial resting solely on the listed grounds.
Article 29 is available to citizens; it does not, by its own text, restrict the special right of minorities to establish and administer their own institutions under Article 30 (a distinct right).
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 29(1) as a group cultural-conservation right and 29(2) as an individual non-discrimination right in education — the two clauses protect different interests and are often pleaded together with Article 30 in minority-institution litigation.

sections.title: Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions
sections.raw_text:
30. Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions.—(1) All minorities, whether based on religion or language, shall have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
(1A) In making any law providing for the compulsory acquisition of any property of an educational institution established and administered by a minority, referred to in clause (1), the State shall ensure that the amount fixed by or determined under such law for the acquisition of such property is such as would not restrict or abrogate the right guaranteed under that clause.
(2) The State shall not, in granting aid to educational institutions, discriminate against any educational institution on the ground that it is under the management of a minority, whether based on religion or language.
key_terms: compulsory acquisition of minority institution property

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 30 is the cornerstone minority-rights provision on education: religious and linguistic minorities have a specific, independent right to found and run their own educational institutions. Clause (1A), inserted in 1978, protects that right from being hollowed out by inadequate compensation if the State compulsorily acquires the institution's property. Clause (2) requires the State to be even-handed when disbursing aid — it cannot discriminate against an institution merely because a minority manages it.
essential_elements: Clause (1): the right-holder is a 'minority' defined by religion or language (not the broader 'any section of citizens' language of Article 29(1)).
Clause (1): the right covers both establishing (founding) and administering (running) educational institutions of the minority's choice.

Clause (1A): where the State compulsorily acquires such an institution's property, the compensation fixed must not restrict or abrogate the clause (1) right — inadequate compensation cannot be used to defeat the right indirectly.
Clause (2): bars discrimination in the grant of State aid to educational institutions on the ground of minority management.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The right to administer is not a right to maladminister — reasonable regulatory measures ensuring educational standards, discipline, and accountability remain permissible even for minority institutions (judicially developed limitation).
Clause (1A) is confined to compulsory acquisition of property of minority educational institutions; it does not touch other forms of regulation.
Clause (2) prohibits discrimination in aid on the specific ground of minority management — it does not compel the State to grant aid to any institution in the first place.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Article 30(1) as creating a distinct, minority-specific institutional right layered on top of the general cultural right in Article 29(1) — and remember clause (1A) exists specifically to prevent compensation law from being used as a backdoor way to defeat clause (1).

sections.title: [Compulsory acquisition of property.] Omitted
sections.raw_text: 31. [Compulsory acquisition of property.]—Omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 6 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 31, which originally guaranteed a fundamental right against compulsory acquisition of property without compensation, was omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, with effect from 20 June 1979 — the same reform that downgraded the right to property from Part III to the ordinary constitutional right under Article 300A.
essential_elements: The article no longer exists in operative form; any reference to it in older case law or statutes should be read as historical.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Superseded by Article 300A (right to property as a constitutional, non-fundamental right) inserted by the same 44th Amendment.
breakdown.how_to_read: Cross-refer to Article 300A for the modern property-right provision, and to Articles 31A-31C (which remain in force) for the surviving saving clauses on land-reform and directive-principle legislation that originally clustered around the old Article 31.

sections.title: Saving of laws providing for acquisition of estates, etc.
sections.raw_text:
31A. Saving of laws providing for acquisition of estates, etc.—(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in article 13, no law providing for—
(a) the acquisition by the State of any estate or of any rights therein or the extinguishment or modification of any such rights, or
(b) the taking over of the management of any property by the State for a limited period either in the public interest or in order to secure the proper management of the property, or
(c) the amalgamation of two or more corporations either in the public interest or in order to secure the proper management of any of the corporations, or
(d) the extinguishment or modification of any rights of managing agents, secretaries and treasurers, managing directors, directors or managers of corporations, or of any voting rights of shareholders thereof, or
(e) the extinguishment or modification of any rights accruing by virtue of any agreement, lease or licence for the purpose of searching for, or winning, any mineral or mineral oil, or the premature termination or cancellation of any such agreement, lease or licence,
shall be deemed to be void on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges any of the rights conferred by article 14 or article 19:
Provided that where such law is a law made by the Legislature of a State, the provisions of this article shall not apply thereto unless such law, having been reserved for the consideration of the President, has received his assent:
Provided further that where any law makes any provision for the acquisition by the State of any estate and where any land comprised therein is held by a person under his personal cultivation, it shall not be lawful for the State to acquire any portion of such land as is within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force or any building or structure standing thereon or appurtenant thereto, unless the law relating to the acquisition of such land, building or structure, provides for payment of compensation at a rate which shall not be less than the market value thereof.
(2) In this article,—
(a) the expression "estate" shall, in relation to any local area, have the same meaning as that expression or its local equivalent has in the existing law relating to land tenures in force in that area and shall also include—
(i) any jagir, inam or muafi or other similar grant and in the States of Tamil Nadu and Kerala, any janmam right;
(ii) any land held under ryotwari settlement;
(iii) any land held or let for purposes of agriculture or for purposes ancillary thereto, including waste land, forest land, land for pasture or sites of buildings and other structures occupied by cultivators of land, agricultural labourers and village artisans;
(b) the expression "rights", in relation to an estate, shall include any rights vesting in a proprietor, sub-proprietor, under-proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyat, under-raiyat or other intermediary and any rights or privileges in respect of land revenue.
key_terms: mineral or mineral oil agreement rights

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 31A immunises a specific, narrow class of land-reform and corporate-management laws from being struck down for conflicting with Articles 14 or 19. It was inserted early (by the First Amendment, 1951) to protect zamindari-abolition and estate-acquisition legislation from constitutional challenge, and was later extended to cover State takeovers of mismanaged property/corporations and mineral-lease terminations. A proviso requires State-legislature laws under this article to have received Presidential assent, and a further proviso protects small cultivators by requiring market-value compensation for land within their personal-cultivation ceiling.
essential_elements: Opens with a non-obstante clause overriding Article 13, and immunises the listed categories of law from challenge under Article 14 or Article 19 specifically (not all of Part III).

Covers five categories of law: (a) acquisition of estates/rights therein, (b) temporary State takeover of property management, (c) amalgamation of corporations, (d) extinguishment of managing agents'/directors'/shareholders' rights, (e) extinguishment of mineral/mineral-oil agreement or lease rights.
First proviso: a State law under this article needs Presidential assent (reservation of the Bill) to attract the article's protection.
Second proviso: protects personal cultivators by requiring market-value compensation for acquisition of land within their statutory ceiling limit, or of buildings/structures on it.

Clause (2) supplies definitions of 'estate' (including jagir, inam, muafi, janmam rights, ryotwari land, and agricultural/ancillary land) and 'rights' (including proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyat, and land-revenue privileges) for the article's purposes.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The immunity runs only against Articles 14 and 19 challenges — the original text also referenced Article 31, but that reference was substituted following Article 31's 1978 omission.
The State-legislature proviso is a condition precedent: without Presidential assent, a State enactment does not get Article 31A's protection even if it otherwise fits one of the five categories.
The personal-cultivation proviso is itself a protective carve-out within the saving clause, ensuring small cultivators still receive fair (market-value) compensation despite the general immunity.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Article 31A as a category-based (not individual-law-based) shield for land-reform and corporate-management legislation — check first whether the law fits one of the five listed categories, then check the assent proviso if it is a State law, then check whether the personal-cultivation proviso's compensation requirement applies.

sections.title: Validation of certain Acts and Regulations
sections.raw_text: 31B. Validation of certain Acts and Regulations.—Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions contained in article 31A, none of the Acts and Regulations specified in the Ninth Schedule nor any of the provisions thereof shall be deemed to be void, or ever to have become void, on the ground that such Act, Regulation or provision is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges any of the rights conferred by, any provisions of this Part, and notwithstanding any judgment, decree or order of any court or Tribunal to the contrary, each of the said Acts and Regulations shall, subject to the power of any competent Legislature to repeal or amend it, continue in force.

breakdown.plain_summary: Article 31B goes further than Article 31A: it individually and retrospectively validates every Act and Regulation specifically listed in the Ninth Schedule, immunising them from challenge under any provision of Part III (not just Articles 14/19), and even overriding any earlier court judgment that had struck them down. It operates in addition to, not instead of, Article 31A's category-based protection.
essential_elements: Protection is instrument-specific — an Act or Regulation must actually be listed in the Ninth Schedule to get Article 31B's immunity, unlike Article 31A's category-based test.
The immunity runs against 'any provisions of this Part' (all of Part III), a wider shield than Article 31A's Article 14/19-only protection.
The validation is retrospective and overrides contrary judicial decisions — a listed Act cannot be treated as having ever been void on Part III grounds.
The listed Legislature retains ordinary power to repeal or amend the protected Act or Regulation — the immunity is from judicial invalidation, not from legislative change.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Judicially qualified by the basic structure doctrine (I.R. Coelho v.
